name: Xhosa
notes:
Xhosa (isiXhosa), a Nguni language of South Africa. Related to Zulu; has /r/ unlike Zulu.

CLICKS. Three click types — dental ⟨c⟩ ǀ, lateral ⟨x⟩ ǁ, postalveolar ⟨q⟩ ǃ — each in six series, giving eighteen click consonants: plain ⟨c⟩ [kǀ], aspirated ⟨ch⟩ [kǀʰ], slack-voiced ⟨gc⟩ [ɡǀ], nasal ⟨nc⟩ [ŋǀ], breathy nasal ⟨ngc⟩ [ŋǀ], and nasal-plus-velar ⟨nkc⟩ [ŋkǀ], with the ⟨x⟩ and ⟨q⟩ rows parallel (xhosa_wiki). Every click carries a rear (velar) closure, so the two-symbol notation kǀ / ŋǀ is the segment, not a cluster (IPA convention for clicks; the superscript variant ᵏǀ found in some sources writes the same segment). ⟨ngc⟩ and ⟨nc⟩ share a surface symbol here: they differ by the breathy/depressor voice quality of the nasal, which this spec does not transcribe (see DEPRESSORS).

STOPS. ⟨b⟩ is the implosive /ɓ/ and ⟨bh⟩ the slack-voiced plosive /b/ — the pair is a spelling contrast, not an aspiration one. ⟨p t k ts tsh tl kr⟩ are ejective in phonetic realisation ([pʼ tʼ kʼ tsʼ tʃʼ tɬʼ kxʼ], xhosa_wiki) and contrast with the aspirated ⟨ph th kh tyh qh ch xh⟩; the grapheme table states the phonemic plain/aspirated contrast and leaves the ejection to the phonetic layer, exactly as it leaves the depressor voice quality.

PALATALS AND LATERALS. ⟨ty⟩ [c], ⟨tyh⟩ [cʰ], ⟨dy⟩ [ɟ] (written t̠ʲʼ, t̠ʲʰ, d̠ʲʱ in narrower sources). ⟨hl⟩ [ɬ], ⟨dl⟩ [ɮ], ⟨tl⟩ [tɬ] are the lateral obstruents; ⟨dl⟩ is a plain fricative, not an affricate. ⟨rh⟩ is the velar fricative [x] and ⟨kr⟩ the velar affricate [kx] (xhosa_wiki). ⟨h⟩ is [h] and ⟨hh⟩ [ɦ]; the source notes that [ɦ] is sometimes spelled ⟨h⟩ as well, and the kaikki transcriptions take that reading throughout — the table here follows the spelling contrast the source's own consonant table draws.

POST-NASAL HARDENING. A class 9/10 nasal prefix hardens a following fricative: ⟨nz⟩ is [ndz] (xhosa_wiki). ⟨mf⟩ and ⟨mv⟩ undergo the same hardening ([ɱpf], [ɱbv]) but only under the class 9 prefix im-; under the class 1/3 prefix um- the same spelling is a syllabic nasal plus a plain fricative (⟨imfene⟩ vs ⟨umfana⟩). The two readings are not distinguishable orthographically, so neither is declared — this is morphology, and it belongs downstream.

MULTIGRAPH KEYS ⟨ntl⟩ ⟨nty⟩ ⟨ndy⟩ ⟨ntsh⟩ ⟨ndl⟩ exist to defeat maximal munch: without them ⟨nt⟩ and ⟨nd⟩ win and ⟨intloko⟩ comes out with a plain /l/ instead of the lateral affricate. They also record the homorganic place of the nasal before a palatal ([ɲc], [ɲɟ], [ɲtʃ]), which is why ⟨nj⟩ is [ɲdʒ] on the same footing.

PROSODY. Tone is phonemic (two levels) but is not written; no rule can recover it from the orthography. Penultimate lengthening IS predictable and is encoded (see the stress block). Words cited in isolation carry a further pre-pausal lengthening, which is why sources transcribe some monosyllables long ([saː], [kǃʰaː]); that is an utterance-level effect and is not encoded, so a monosyllable — having no penult — comes out short.

DEPRESSORS. The slack-voiced obstruents ⟨bh d g v z j dl gc gq gx ngc ngq ngx⟩ lower the pitch of the following vowel and are transcribed in narrow work with a devoicing ring on the consonant and breathy voice on the vowel ([íb̥ǎ̤ːsi] ⟨ibhasi⟩); Jessen & Roux (2002) is the acoustic study. This spec writes the broad voiced symbols and leaves the voice-quality detail to a phonetic layer.

NOT ENCODED: mid-vowel height alternation ([e]~[ɛ], [o]~[ɔ]) conditioned by the following vowel, and the syllabic nasal of the class 1/3 prefix um- — both need information the spelling does not carry, or a morphological analysis.

sources.author: Larry M. Hyman
sources.title: Penultimate lengthening in Bantu: Analysis and spread
sources.publisher: John Benjamins (Language Typology and Historical Contingency, eds. Bickel, Grenoble, Peterson & Timberlake)
sources.notes: Quotes Doke (1967: 94) on Nguni penultimate stress and length. Its Table 1 shows most of the surveyed Bantu languages, Ndebele included, lengthening monosyllables pre-pausally; Shekgalagari is the exception. The paper therefore supports the penult claim, not a monosyllable exemption.

sources.author: Michael Jessen and Justus C. Roux
sources.title: Voice quality differences associated with stops and clicks in Xhosa
sources.notes: Acoustic study of the Xhosa depressor/slack-voice series; abstract and bibliographic record consulted, full text not consulted.

allophone_rules.notes: ⟨w⟩ after a consonant is secondary rounding on that consonant rather than a separate glide segment — ⟨incwadi⟩ [iŋǀʷaːdi], ⟨umnqweno⟩ [umŋǃʷeːno], ⟨krwe⟩ [kxʷe]. The Xhosa orthography source (xhosa_wiki) declares no labialised series in its consonant table; what it does is write the diacritic on the consonant wherever a ⟨w⟩ follows one, in its palatalisation examples ([ukukotʃʷa], [ukupʰutʃʰʷa]). The kaikki transcriptions write it the same way throughout.

Penultimate lengthening targets the PENULT, so a word-final vowel is never long: ⟨molo⟩ is [moːlo], not *[moːloː], and the monosyllables ⟨fa⟩ and ⟨lo⟩ have no penult to lengthen at all. Undoes the nucleus_stressed lengthening wherever the orthographic syllable count puts the last vowel of the word inside the stressed nucleus (a vowel run such as ⟨oo⟩ is one nucleus spelled with two letters). Isolation forms in the literature are also pre-pausally lengthened (Hyman 2013), an utterance-level effect this spec does not model.

stress.notes: Nguni prominence is penultimate: "Stress in Nguni [Xhosa, Zulu, Swati, Ndebele] is normally on the penultimate syllable which is also normally long" (Doke 1967: 94, quoted in Hyman 2013). The prominence is realised as length rather than as an accentual mark, so stress_mark is empty and the length is written by the nucleus_stressed entries in positional_graphemes. vowel_letters is declared because ⟨y⟩ and ⟨w⟩ are consonants here: without it the bundled syllabifier reads ⟨oya⟩ as one nucleus and the length lands on the wrong vowel, or on two.
